ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: in the figure there is a horizontal line labeled as the equator, and a vertical meridian labeled as 20°E; the two lines intersect at point O; point P is on the equator and located to the left of point O, that is, west of point O; point Q is on the 20°E meridian and located below point O, that is, in the Southern Hemisphere direction. Then reason: let arc OP=arc OQ=x°. From the figure, P is on the equator, so latitude φ_P=0°; Q is south of O and arc OQ=x°, so latitude φ_Q=-x°. The formula for noon solar altitude is H=90°-|φ-δ|. The stem says the noon solar altitudes of P and Q are equal, therefore 90°-|0-δ|=90°-|-x-δ|, namely |δ|=|-x-δ|. Since x>0, solving gives δ=-x/2, indicating that the subsolar point is in the Southern Hemisphere. When the Sun directly shines on the Southern Hemisphere, it is the winter half-year in the Northern Hemisphere; the Earth is close to perihelion, and its orbital speed is relatively fast.
